# SpaceX Daily
> **A Starlink satellite dropped 12 km then climbed back, showing how the constellation corrects sudden orbital decay.**

### Top News

1. **Starlink Satellite Recovers From Sudden 12 km Drop**
   STARLINK-35829 dropped 12 km before climbing back to its original altitude. The event highlights the satellite’s ability to execute recovery maneuvers after an unexpected decay. The maneuver demonstrates the satellite’s onboard propulsion system responding to transient atmospheric drag without requiring immediate ground intervention. KeepTrack tracked the altitude change and subsequent restoration in real time. Source: [keeptrack.space](https://keeptrack.space/satellite-of-the-day/sotd-2026-11-24)

2. **Northrop Grumman Contracts Extra Falcon 9 for Cygnus**
   Northrop Grumman booked one additional Falcon 9 for a Cygnus cargo mission. The move confirms Antares 330 remains unavailable for near-term launches. Dave Schiller of Northrop Grumman stated during a NASA teleconference that the company had secured the extra Falcon 9. This decision follows repeated delays in Antares development and ensures continued ISS cargo delivery cadence. The Falcon 9 will handle the NG-25 mission no earlier than November 29. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/SciGuySpace/status/2124920065367699555)

3. **Profepa Reports 5.9 kg of Debris Collected After Starship Test**
   Mexico’s Profepa collected 5.9 kilograms of material at Playa Bagdad following the November 13 Starship test. High tides, wind, and limited access slowed recovery efforts. SpaceX stated its partners found very few fragments and questioned their origin. Conibio Global separately counted more than 1,500 pieces along roughly two kilometers of beach. Profepa advised the public not to handle any found material and to report discoveries through official channels. The agency is reviewing technical information SpaceX submitted about the vehicle’s materials. Source: [neoteo.com](https://www.neoteo.com/en/profepa-reports-59-kg-of-waste-collected-after-starship-test-in-mexico)

4. **Britain Seeks Answers on Starshield Service Changes**
   British officials demanded explanations from SpaceX after October restrictions affected Ukraine’s Starshield service. The changes reportedly included renewed limits over occupied territories. Jim Himes requested written responses from Elon Musk and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. CNN reported two separate rounds of speed restrictions lasting several weeks in total. Accounts differ on whether SpaceX or U.S. government officials initiated the limits. Source: [neoteo.com](https://www.neoteo.com/en/himes-ties-his-support-for-spacex-funding-to-starshield-answers)

5. **SpaceX Moves to Wholesale Rideshare Model**
   SpaceX is shifting its rideshare offerings toward a wholesale approach. The change alters how smaller payloads secure secondary launch slots. Secondary payload customers will now purchase capacity in bulk rather than individual slots. The model aims to streamline manifest management as Falcon 9 flight rate remains high. Source: [advanced-television.com](https://www.advanced-television.com/2026/11/24/spacex-shifts-to-wholesale-rideshare-model/)

6. **Elon Musk Outlines Plans for Larger Starship**
   Elon Musk stated SpaceX is already designing a bigger Starship variant. The effort targets increased payload capacity beyond current Block 3 vehicles. The new configuration would build on lessons from recent flight tests and tower catch operations. Musk indicated the design work is underway even as Block 3 vehicles continue production. Source: [aero-news.net](https://www.aero-news.net/index.cfm?do=main.textpost&id=AFC05AA2-F449-4A13-B91A-15452E5A571E)

   All four Cursor co-founders appeared on the list of the world’s youngest self-made billionaires. The recognition follows the company’s growth after its tie to the SpaceX ecosystem through Anysphere. Cursor’s valuation has risen rapidly as the AI code editor integrates multiple frontier models. The four founders each hold equity positions that reflect the platform’s adoption among developers. Source: [app.dealroom.co](https://app.dealroom.co/news/note/cursor-s-four-co-founders-on-list-of-the-world-s-youngest-self-made-billionaires)

   Representative Jim Himes requested written explanations from Elon Musk and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Starshield service changes. CNN noted that service limits over occupied Ukrainian territories resumed after an initial period of relaxation. Himes is expected to become chair of the House Intelligence Committee in January 2027. ### Engineering Deep Dive
The 12 km altitude loss recorded by STARLINK-35829 offers a clear window into low-Earth orbit drag mechanics. At typical Starlink altitudes near 550 km, residual atmospheric density still exerts measurable force; even small increases in that density from solar activity or orbital positioning raise drag enough to drop a satellite several kilometers in days. The satellite’s subsequent climb back demonstrates the Hall-effect thrusters’ ability to restore the original orbit without ground intervention beyond initial commands. Recovery performance depends on propellant reserves and thrust-to-mass ratio. Each Starlink satellite carries a modest krypton load sized for station-keeping and collision-avoidance burns; a 12 km correction consumes only a fraction of that budget yet proves the system can absorb transient decay events. Scaling this capability across thousands of satellites keeps the constellation’s relative spacing intact even when individual units experience unexpected drag spikes.

The same propulsion architecture that enables these recoveries also sets the margin for future constellation growth. Higher drag environments at slightly lower altitudes would shorten satellite life unless propellant margins or thrust efficiency improve. The observed 12 km excursion and recovery therefore functions as an in-orbit calibration point for both drag models and the minimum impulse needed to protect overall constellation geometry. Engineers can now compare the actual impulse used against pre-flight predictions to refine solar-activity forecasting tools. This data loop directly informs how many additional satellites must be launched each year to maintain coverage as the constellation expands.

Propellant budgeting at constellation scale reveals a second-order constraint. Every kilogram of krypton reserved for recovery burns reduces the mass available for station-keeping over the satellite’s design life. The 12 km event shows that the current margin is sufficient for isolated incidents, yet repeated events during solar maximum would accumulate. SpaceX can respond by raising average operating altitude, increasing thruster efficiency, or accepting slightly shorter satellite lifetimes. Each choice carries a different cost in launch cadence and constellation replenishment rate. The single satellite’s measured recovery therefore supplies a concrete data point that feeds directly into fleet-wide economic models.
